title: Psychology
blurb: Biases, memory, habits, social influence and emotions.

lessons.title: Thinking traps
lessons.summary: The mental shortcuts that fool everyone.

cards.title: Two systems
cards.text: Psychologist Daniel Kahneman described two modes of thinking. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive. System 2 is slow, effortful and logical. Most biases come from System 1 answering before System 2 checks.

cards.title: Confirmation bias
cards.text: We notice, remember and trust information that agrees with what we already believe, and dismiss what doesn't. It's why two people can read the same news and both feel proven right.

cards.title: Anchoring
cards.text: The first number you hear pulls your estimate towards it, even if it's random. A jacket "reduced from €300 to €120" feels cheap because €300 became the anchor.

cards.title: Availability heuristic
cards.text: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes make the news, so flying feels riskier than driving, though per kilometre it's far safer.

cards.title: Sunk cost fallacy

items.r: "Is it worth it from now on?"

cards.text: We keep investing in something because of what we've already spent, not because of what's to come. Finishing a bad film because you paid for the ticket is a classic case.

cards.title: Loss aversion
cards.text: Losing €50 hurts roughly twice as much as winning €50 feels good. That's why people take big risks to avoid a loss but play safe to protect a gain.

cards.title: The Dunning–Kruger effect
cards.text: People with a little knowledge often overrate their skill, because they don't yet know what they don't know. As expertise grows, confidence first dips, then rises with real skill.

cards.title: Survivorship bias
cards.text: We study the winners and forget the failures we can't see. "Drop out of university like the famous founders" ignores the thousands who dropped out and didn't succeed.

cards.title: The framing effect
cards.text: The same fact feels different depending on the wording. Patients choose a surgery with a "90% survival rate" far more often than one with a "10% death rate", though they're identical.

cards.title: Beating your biases

items: Ask what would change your mind
Set your budget before seeing prices

cards.text: You can't switch biases off, but you can slow down for important choices: look for opposing evidence, ask "what would change my mind?", and decide before you see the anchor.

quiz.q: A shop shows "was €300, now €120". Which bias makes it feel cheap?
Keeping a bad investment because of what you already paid is the…
quiz.explain: Only future costs and benefits matter.

quiz.q: Roughly how much more does a loss hurt than an equal gain?
quiz.explain: Loss aversion, measured by Kahneman and Tversky.

lessons.title: How memory works
lessons.summary: Why you forget, and how to remember better.

cards.title: Three stages
cards.text: Memory has three stages: encoding (taking information in), storage (keeping it) and retrieval (getting it back). Most "forgetting" is actually a failure to encode or retrieve.

cards.title: Short-term vs long-term
cards.text: Working memory holds only a few items for seconds, about 4 chunks. Long-term memory has practically no limit and can last a lifetime.

cards.title: The forgetting curve
cards.text: Hermann Ebbinghaus showed in 1885 that we forget fast: much of new material is gone within a day unless we review it. Each review flattens the curve.

cards.title: Spaced repetition
cards.text: Reviewing just before you'd forget is the most efficient way to learn. Intervals grow each time: 1 day, 3 days, a week, a month. This app's review queue uses the same idea.

cards.title: Active recall
cards.text: Testing yourself beats rereading. Trying to pull an answer out of memory strengthens it far more than looking at it again, even when you get it wrong.

cards.title: Chunking
cards.text: We remember more by grouping items into meaningful chunks. A phone number like 912345678 is easier as 912 345 678, and chess masters see board patterns, not single pieces.

cards.title: Sleep and memory
cards.text: During deep sleep the brain replays the day's experiences and moves them into long-term storage. Pulling an all-nighter before an exam hurts the very memories you need.

cards.title: False memories
cards.text: Memories are rebuilt every time we recall them, so they can change. Elizabeth Loftus showed that a leading question ("how fast were the cars when they smashed?") alters what witnesses remember.

cards.title: The memory palace
cards.text: An ancient technique: imagine a familiar place and put each item to remember at a spot along a route. Walking the route in your mind brings the items back. Memory champions use it.

cards.title: A study plan that works
cards.text: Combine the tricks: short sessions, test yourself, space the reviews and sleep. Ten minutes a day with this app beats two hours once a week.

quiz.q: Which study method strengthens memory most?
Why is an all-nighter bad before an exam?
quiz.explain: Deep sleep moves learning into long-term memory.

lessons.title: Habits and motivation
lessons.summary: Why we do what we do, and how to change it.

cards.title: The habit loop
cards.text: Habits run on a loop: a cue triggers a routine, which brings a reward. Over time the brain links the cue to the reward and runs the routine automatically.

cards.title: Make it easy
cards.text: Small friction changes behaviour a lot. Put the fruit on the counter and the biscuits in a high cupboard; lay out your running shoes the night before.

cards.title: Tiny habits
cards.text: Start absurdly small: one push-up, one page, two minutes. Small wins build identity ("I'm someone who exercises"), and it's easier to grow a habit than to start one.

cards.title: Habit stacking
cards.text: Attach a new habit to an existing one: "After I pour my morning coffee, I'll write three lines in my journal." The old habit becomes the cue.

cards.title: Intrinsic vs extrinsic
cards.text: Intrinsic motivation comes from enjoying the thing itself; extrinsic from rewards or pressure. Paying people for something they already enjoy can sometimes reduce their interest.

cards.title: Self-determination theory
cards.text: Psychologists Deci and Ryan found three needs that fuel lasting motivation: autonomy (choice), competence (getting better) and relatedness (connection with others).

cards.title: Dopamine
cards.text: Dopamine is less about pleasure and more about wanting and anticipation. It spikes when we expect a reward, which is why notifications and endless feeds are so gripping.

cards.title: Delayed gratification
cards.text: In the famous "marshmallow test", children could eat one treat now or wait for two. Later studies suggest family background and trust explain much of who waits.

cards.title: Flow
cards.text: Flow is the state of total absorption, when time disappears. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi found it happens when a challenge matches your skill, neither too easy nor too hard.

cards.title: Building a reading habit
cards.text: Cue: after dinner. Routine: read one page on the sofa, phone in another room. Reward: tick it on a calendar. Two months later, it's automatic.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of the habit loop?

quiz.explain: Too easy is boring; too hard causes anxiety.

lessons.title: Social psychology
lessons.summary: How other people change what we think and do.

cards.title: Conformity
cards.text: In Solomon Asch's 1950s experiments, people judged which line matched another. When actors all gave the wrong answer, many participants went along at least once.

cards.title: Obedience to authority
cards.text: Stanley Milgram's 1960s experiment found many ordinary people would give what they believed were dangerous electric shocks when an authority figure told them to continue. No shocks were real.

cards.title: The bystander effect
cards.text: The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help: each assumes someone else will. Pointing at one person, "you, call 112!", breaks the spell.

cards.title: Social proof
cards.text: When unsure, we copy others. Reviews, queues outside restaurants and "best-seller" labels all work because we assume many people can't be wrong.

cards.title: The halo effect
cards.text: One good trait colours our view of everything else. Attractive or confident people are often judged as smarter or kinder, without evidence.

cards.title: In-groups and out-groups
cards.text: We easily split the world into "us" and "them", even based on trivial things like a coin toss, and then favour our own group. Sports rivalries show it every weekend.

cards.title: Cognitive dissonance
cards.text: Holding two clashing beliefs feels uncomfortable, so we change one. A smoker who knows smoking kills may tell themselves "my grandad smoked and lived to 90".

cards.title: Reciprocity
cards.text: We feel obliged to return favours. A free sample, a small gift or a waiter's mint makes people more likely to buy or tip.

cards.title: The spotlight effect

viz.unit: % of people who noticed the shirt

cards.text: We think others notice our mistakes and appearance far more than they do. In one study, students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed half the room noticed; far fewer did.

cards.title: Using it for good

items: "Most guests in this room reuse towels"

cards.text: Social psychology isn't just about manipulation. Hotels that said "most guests reuse their towels" got more towel reuse than those that appealed to the environment.

quiz.q: Why do crowds sometimes fail to help in an emergency?
Long queues outside a restaurant persuade us through…
quiz.explain: We assume many people can't be wrong.

lessons.title: Emotions and wellbeing
lessons.summary: What feelings are for, and what science says about happiness.

cards.title: Basic emotions
cards.text: Paul Ekman found six emotions with facial expressions recognised across cultures: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust.

cards.title: What emotions are for
cards.text: Emotions are fast signals that prepare the body to act: fear to escape, anger to defend, disgust to avoid poison, sadness to seek support.

cards.title: Fight or flight
cards.text: In danger, the amygdala triggers adrenaline: the heart races, breathing speeds up and muscles get ready. Useful against a bear, less so before a presentation.

cards.title: Naming emotions
cards.text: Putting a feeling into words ("I'm anxious about tomorrow") reduces activity in the brain's alarm system. Psychologists call it affect labelling.

cards.title: The hedonic treadmill
cards.text: After a raise, a new car or even a lottery win, happiness tends to drift back to its usual level. We quickly adapt to good things, and fairly well to many bad ones.

cards.title: What predicts happiness
cards.text: Harvard's long-running study of adult development, started in 1938, found one strong predictor of health and happiness in old age: warm, close relationships.

cards.title: Gratitude
cards.text: Writing down three good things each day, or thanking someone in a letter, reliably boosts mood in studies. It trains attention to notice what's going well.

cards.title: Exercise and mood
cards.text: Regular exercise works on mood about as well as some treatments for mild low mood, and it improves sleep and focus. Even a 10-minute walk helps.

cards.title: Growth mindset
cards.text: Carol Dweck's idea: believing abilities can be developed, rather than fixed, helps people keep going after setbacks. "I can't do this yet" beats "I'm not good at this".

cards.title: A 2-minute reset
cards.text: When stress spikes: breathe out longer than you breathe in (in for 4, out for 6) for a minute, name the feeling, then pick one small next step. Long exhales calm the nervous system.
